reviews.original_attached_text: Karmokar and coauthors survey capacitor and transistor common-centroid (CC) methods, then examine cases where clustered or interdigitated patterns perform better. Their argument is physical: CC removes a particular systematic error term, while potentially introducing resistance imbalance and layout-dependent device shifts. The review is evidence for a conditional pattern choice , not for either a universal CC rule or a universal rejection of CC. Introduction, PDF p. 1 §V, PDF pp. 6–7
reviews.supported_claim: Common-centroid layouts can lose to other patterns when routing and layout-dependent shifts dominate; selection depends on circuit and process.
reviews.detail: §I and §V give the motivation, source-current/LOD mechanisms, and OTA/comparator case studies. These are conditional examples, not a universal size threshold. Engine candidate-selection policies are handbook synthesis.

reviews.original_attached_text: Let an equal unit of device A or B sample a parameter field p(x,y)=p₀+gₓx+gᵧy . The mean parameter difference is gₓ(x̄A−x̄B)+gᵧ(ȳA−ȳB) . Coincident centroids remove this term for every gradient direction. To translate parameter matching into output matching, the review additionally linearizes performance as ΔP≈(∂P/∂p)Δp . These are two distinct approximations: spatial variation and circuit response. Equations (1)–(5), PDF p. 1
reviews.supported_claim: Coincident normalized first moments cancel a linear parameter field; circuit response is separately linearized.
reviews.detail: Eqs.(1)–(5) support equal-unit centroid and sensitivity statements. Arbitrary unequal electrical weights and software certificates are explicitly handbook extensions under an additive model.

reviews.original_attached_text: The review separates global, local spatially correlated, and local uncorrelated variation. Its correlation models and mismatch coefficients are process parameters. Layout can change correlated differential error; rearranging identical independent random units at fixed total active area does not make their intrinsic randomness disappear. Global variation cancels in a difference only to the extent that the compared devices and circuit sensitivities respond alike. §II, PDF pp. 2–3
reviews.supported_claim: Variation has global, local uncorrelated and local correlated components; differential variance depends on correlation.
reviews.detail: §II supplies variation/covariance models. The compact dᵀΣd identity is derived covariance algebra; its matrix-validity and common-sample validation policy are handbook guidance.

reviews.original_attached_text: §II-A2 and Fig. 2, PDF p. 2 The review's statement that identical units remove several LDEs depends on its row-based, uniform-pitch, diffusion-sharing construction. Philis must verify those premises before reusing that conclusion. A dummy of the wrong layer or an electrically floating active dummy is not equivalent to the characterized boundary environment.
reviews.supported_claim: WPE, LOD, OD spacing and pitch depend on actual surrounding geometry; the review’s uniform-row claims have construction premises.
reviews.detail: §II-A2 and Fig.2 checked. Removed a blanket assertion that floating active dummies are invalid; their accepted bias depends on the qualified construction.

reviews.original_attached_text: For transistor arrays, diffusion sharing, source connection resistance, and gate/drain access constrain viable CC patterns. The review describes half-diffusion graphs and Euler paths for constructing diffusion-sharing arrays, then routing that accounts for electromigration and IR drop. These methods provide useful internal macro representations, but capacitor placement algorithms cannot simply be applied to MOS arrays: their adjacency constraints are different. §IV, PDF pp. 5–6
reviews.supported_claim: Transistor array construction uses half-diffusion graphs/Euler connectivity and current-aware routing.
reviews.detail: §IV supports this transistor-specific construction; it is not a capacitor-placement algorithm.

reviews.original_attached_text: A source lead carrying small-signal current creates local source degeneration. For a simple single-branch model, gₘ,eff≈gₘ/(1+gₘRₛ) ; the review analyzes actual unit-current distribution through the array. Wider wires or a different connection tree can improve transconductance, while unequal resistance can create offset. Equal total drawn length does not guarantee equal terminal impedance because layers, vias, branch loading, and neighbors differ. Equation (25) and Fig. 9, PDF pp. 6–7
reviews.supported_claim: Local source impedance changes effective transconductance according to unit currents and connection topology.
reviews.detail: Eq.(25)/Fig.9 support the mechanism. gm/(1+gmRs) is explicitly derived here for a single branch neglecting body effect/output conductance; it is not copied as Eq.(25).

reviews.original_attached_text: The review compares MOM finger, sandwich, pillar, and mortise-tenon structures, their density, and their ability to suppress unwanted top-plate coupling. Its preference for MOM in the discussed advanced-node setting is not a universal replacement rule for an available, characterized MIM device. Unit structure determines which parasitics are exposed to the router. §III and Fig. 4, PDF pp. 3–5
reviews.supported_claim: MOM unit structures differ in capacitance density and unwanted top-plate coupling.
reviews.detail: Corrected Fig.4/PDF3 reference to §III-B Fig.5/PDF4. The previous span contained the figure but mislabeled it.

reviews.original_attached_text: The paper surveys ILP, pair-sequence search, chessboard construction, and routing-aware stochastic approaches. Retain exclusivity, exact unit ratios, channel capacity, and connectivity as explicit invariants. A visually regular pattern with no legal route is not a usable placement. §III-C, PDF pp. 4–5 See the 2023 DAC paper for a concrete constructive alternative.
reviews.supported_claim: Capacitor-layout methods impose ratios/exclusivity and address dispersion/routing jointly.
reviews.detail: §III-C surveys ILP, pair-sequence, chessboard and routing-aware methods. Proposed Philis invariants remain adaptations.

reviews.original_attached_text: The review's OTA example combines CC for larger structures with a clustered small mirror; its comparator example exposes how small structures can suffer from CC parasitic/LDE mismatch. Those examples establish the existence of the tradeoff, not a size threshold transferable to SKY130. §V-B, PDF p. 7

reviews.original_attached_text: Source finding: design centering means yield optimization in parameter space. It is unrelated to putting devices at the geometric center of a floorplan. Common-centroid placement can improve one physical contributor to yield, but is not itself design centering. The book makes the distinction even between centering performance values, inscribing the largest tolerance ellipsoid, and maximizing actual probability mass. PDF pp. 89–99 , pp. 164–166 , p. 179 .
reviews.supported_claim: Design centering maximizes probability mass satisfying electrical specifications; centering performance, inscribing an ellipsoid and maximizing yield are distinct.
reviews.detail: §4.8, Eq. (114), PDF89; §4.8.5 PDF96–99; §7.1.2–7.1.3 PDF164–166; §7.2.4 PDF179. The geometric-placement contrast is explanatory terminology, not a separate source theorem.

reviews.original_attached_text: The book writes performance as f(xd, xs, xr) . Design parameters xd are quantities the designer controls: device dimensions, bias choices and, in a layout extension, legal placement coordinates, fingers, topology, widths and contacts. Statistical parameters xs represent manufacturing variation and have a probability model. Range parameters xr represent operating conditions such as supply and temperature; their specified ranges must be covered, and a probability distribution need not exist. Treating range parameters as convenient random variables silently changes the specification. PDF pp. 46–50 .
reviews.supported_claim: Design, statistical and operating-range parameters have different roles; the RC teaching example has different performance-centered and parameter-centered solutions.
reviews.detail: §§2.1–2.5 PDF38–44, Eqs. (3)–(4); §§3.1–3.5 PDF46–50. Recomputed sqrt(1.25), ((sqrt(.5)+sqrt(2))/2)^2=1.125. The normalized area R+C is explicitly an illustrative model.

reviews.original_attached_text: The introductory circuit uses normalized parameters with time constant τ = RC and illustrative area A = R + C . Centering the allowed time-constant interval [0.5, 2] gives τ = 1.25; minimum illustrative area then gives R = C = √1.25. Centering the feasible segment along R = C instead gives R = C = (√0.5 + √2)/2 and τ = 1.125. Unequal R and C standard deviations change the yield optimum again. This is a pedagogical normalized model, not a physical claim that resistance and capacitance can be added to obtain silicon area. PDF pp. 38–44 .

reviews.original_attached_text: For mean μ and covariance C, a multivariate Gaussian is characterized by squared distance β² = (xs − μ)ᵀC⁻¹(xs − μ) . With diagonal standard-deviation matrix D and correlation matrix R, C = DRD . A factorization C = AAᵀ allows samples xs = μ + Az with independent standard-normal components in z. Whitening also makes numerical distances meaningful when parameters have different units. PDF pp. 51–63 .
reviews.supported_claim: Positive-definite covariance defines Mahalanobis contours; covariance factorization preserves shared and local variation.
reviews.detail: §§3.6–3.9 PDF53–64, Eqs. (24), (26), (56)–(60). PSD validation, reduced-rank sampling and the shared-term difference example are sound numerical/linear-algebra extensions; source pairwise-correlation conditions alone are not a complete PD test. Added explicit positive-definite assumption to inverse formula.

reviews.original_attached_text: Global and local variations must remain separate. A global threshold perturbation shared by two matched transistors largely cancels in their difference; independent local threshold errors do not. Under a simple model q1 = μ1 + g + l1 , q2 = μ2 + g + l2 , independent local terms with variance σl² give Var(q1 − q2) = 2σl² . Counting g independently twice destroys that cancellation. Conversely, assuming every local effect is independent discards spatial correlations. The book introduces global/local decomposition; the exact decomposition used by an engine must come from the PDK or a calibrated model. PDF pp. 63–64 .

reviews.original_attached_text: A local sensitivity matrix has entries Sij = ∂fi/∂xj , giving Δf ≈ SΔx . Rows describe how one output responds to all parameters; columns describe one parameter's effects on all outputs. The book uses these directions to discuss similarity, significance and adjustability. Their numerical lengths and angles are meaningful only after defining parameter and performance scales. Changing nanometers to micrometers must not alter which transistor appears important. PDF pp. 68–75 .
reviews.supported_claim: Sensitivities are local derivatives requiring consistent scaling; Pareto dominance uses every retained objective, and weighted sums can miss nonconvex-front portions.
reviews.detail: §§4.1–4.3 PDF68–75, Eqs. (71)–(91); §4.5 PDF75–83, Eqs. (94)–(100). The implementation and normalization advice is a derived recommendation. No global-optimality guarantee follows from a gradient.

reviews.original_attached_text: Pareto dominance compares a complete objective vector: one candidate dominates another only if it is no worse in every retained objective and strictly better in at least one. Weighted sums can miss unsupported portions of nonconvex fronts. Min-max or target-based formulations can explore other compromises, but their weights and reference points still encode user preferences. A zero-weight objective can permit weakly Pareto solutions; retain tie-breaking and dominance checks. PDF pp. 75–83 .

reviews.original_attached_text: Box case. Let f ≈ f0 + gᵀδ and independent bounded coordinates satisfy |δk| ≤ ak. Then the upper linear worst case is f0 + Σ|gk|ak ; choose δk = ak sign(gk). The lower case changes the sign. This is appropriate for a specified independent tolerance box and exact for a linear response. If gk = 0, that coordinate is undetermined to first order; it is not proven irrelevant to a nonlinear circuit. PDF pp. 103–108 .
reviews.supported_claim: Linear box and ellipsoid extrema have different closed forms; nonlinear extrema can be interior or nonunique and local SQP does not certify a global worst case.

reviews.original_attached_text: Nonlinear case. Optimize the real response over the statistical region and operating range. Different specifications generally have different worst-case points; an interior operating point can be worse than all corners. Mismatch can produce multiple opposite failure directions. A single start of an SQP solver is not a global certificate. The book explicitly discusses these difficulties and the nested cost of worst-case analysis. PDF pp. 87–89 , pp. 113–124 , pp. 147–153 .

reviews.original_attached_text: One sample passes only if every specified feature passes throughout the required operating domain. A gain pass probability and a phase-margin pass probability are yield partitions. Their minimum is an upper bound on joint yield; multiplying them is justified only with independence. Because the same devices and parasitics influence both outputs, independence is usually a modeling assumption to test, not a default. PDF pp. 89–96 .
reviews.supported_claim: Yield is an intersection event; a Gaussian half-space, interval, box and ellipsoid have different probabilities; one tangent failure surface is only a local nonlinear approximation.
reviews.detail: §4.8.1–4.8.4 PDF89–96; §§6.2.2–6.2.4 PDF133–145, Eqs. (240), (242)–(248), (258)–(259); §6.3 PDF146–160. Table11 PDF138 gives 46.8% for n=10,beta=3. The 1–3% claim at PDF156 is historical empirical experience, correctly not promoted to a bound.

reviews.original_attached_text: A β = 3 statement needs a region definition. For one linear upper-bounded Gaussian output it corresponds to Φ(3), about 99.865% passing. For a symmetric interval on that output it gives 2Φ(3) − 1. For an n-dimensional Gaussian ellipsoid of radius β, enclosed probability is Pr[χ²n ≤ β²] , not Φ(β). The book's table shows that a radius-three ellipsoid encloses about 46.8% in ten dimensions. There is no contradiction: a half-space and a ball are different events. PDF pp. 133–145 .

reviews.original_attached_text: Geometric yield analysis finds the nearest failure boundary in whitened coordinates. Linearizing that boundary at its most probable point gives a half-space approximation and a signed distance: positive for nominally passing, negative for nominally failing. This is more informative than nominal slack alone because it divides a performance margin by sensitivity to variation. However, curved or disconnected boundaries and multiple failure regions can invalidate a single tangent approximation. The book's 1–3% empirical approximation discussion is historical experience, not a guaranteed error bound for Philis or a justification for ppm certification. PDF pp. 146–160 .

reviews.original_attached_text: With N independent process samples and K passing samples, Ŷ = K/N . For Bernoulli pass events, Var(Ŷ) = Y(1−Y)/N . The variance depends directly on sample count and yield, while the cost per sample still depends on circuit size, parameter count and operating checks. Accuracy improving like 1/√N explains why a visually convincing handful of simulations cannot validate high yield. PDF pp. 125–133 .
reviews.supported_claim: Ordinary Monte Carlo uses Bernoulli sampling; importance sampling uses density ratios and different variance accounting.
reviews.detail: §6.1 PDF125–133, Eqs. (219), (223)–(226). No-failure confidence limits and support warnings are derived estimator safeguards; independently recomputed, not quoted as book equations.

reviews.original_attached_text: The book's importance-sampling estimator reweights draws from a proposal q by p/q. A proposal must cover all relevant failure support; otherwise omitted failure modes create bias. For rare failures, estimating failure probability directly can be more stable than subtracting a yield estimate from one. Record weights, effective sample behavior and the proposal. A variance formula for unweighted Bernoulli samples cannot be reused unchanged for weighted samples. PDF pp. 127–132 .

reviews.original_attached_text: For fixed Gaussian covariance and a fixed acceptance region, the book derives the mean-shift yield gradient ∇μY = YC⁻¹(μaccepted − μ) . This explains the term centering: at an unconstrained stationary point with positive yield, the accepted population's mean matches the manufactured population's mean. It is not a sufficient global optimality condition. More importantly, transistor width, routing topology or finger count generally changes the acceptance region and may change covariance; the formula cannot be applied to those design variables as if they simply shifted a process distribution. PDF pp. 162–170 .

reviews.original_attached_text: The geometric alternative improves signed worst-case distances. A min-max formulation maximizes the weakest distance; a target least-squares formulation balances distances against chosen goals. This can deliberately trade nominal bandwidth for better weak metrics. The source op-amp example raises the minimum distance from 1.1 to 3.9 while reducing nominal transit frequency; it illustrates robust tradeoffs, not an engine-independent guarantee. PDF pp. 173–180 .

reviews.original_attached_text: For a local residual vector e and Jacobian J, the regularized least-squares step solves (JᵀJ + λI)r = −Jᵀe . The transpose on the right is essential; the printed equations 365 and 368 omit it despite defining gradients as rows. Use numerically stable QR/SVD or an appropriate solver rather than blindly forming normal equations when conditioning is poor. Verify predicted improvement by re-evaluating the true response and shrink the trust region if agreement deteriorates. This prevents large geometry moves from exploiting an obsolete local model. PDF pp. 175–179 .

reviews.original_attached_text: The authors target binary-weighted and split charge-scaling DACs, especially a commercial 12 nm process with high wire/via resistance and directional routing. The unit count of a conventional N-bit bank with its grounded dummy is 2 N ; a split topology uses two smaller banks and an attenuation capacitor. That architecture reduces unit count but introduces a particularly sensitive bridge element and separate top-plate nodes. Layout generation must preserve the supplied architecture. §I–II, PDF pp. 1–3
reviews.supported_claim: The DAC paper targets binary/split charge-scaling arrays and evaluates models in a commercial 12 nm process.
reviews.detail: Retained architecture discussion at pp1–3; added §V/PDF10 for the commercial-process setup omitted by the old citation.

reviews.original_attached_text: The model separates intended capacitor values, top-to-bottom parasitics, top-to-substrate parasitics, and bottom-plate loading. The first two can perturb effective ratios; shunt loading and interconnect resistance influence power and settling. Coupling depends on excitation: two terminals at equal potential exchange no incremental charge through their mutual capacitor in that excitation, but this does not mean the physical coupling vanishes under every transition. §II, PDF pp. 2–3
reviews.supported_claim: Binary and split DACs have distinct top-plate graphs and several parasitic classes with different static/dynamic effects.
reviews.detail: §II, especially §II-B, supports terminal distinctions under the paper’s switch/output assumptions. Full reference/switch/amplifier acceptance tests are proposed extensions.

reviews.original_attached_text: §IV-A, PDF pp. 7–8
reviews.supported_claim: Spiral, chessboard and block chessboard constructions trade connected same-bit clusters against dispersion.
reviews.detail: §IV-A and placement figures checked. No universal pattern ranking is inferred.

reviews.original_attached_text: The unit-count exception is significant: C₀ and C₁ each have one unit in the binary bank, so they cannot both individually occupy the same centroid in a nonoverlapping grid. The paper places them near the center. Call this an approximation for those members, not an exact all-member CC certificate. Split banks have analogous odd-count and bridge-placement exceptions. Odd-count exception, PDF p. 7 Split placement, PDF p. 9
reviews.supported_claim: The two one-unit members are placed near the center as a stated exception to exact common-centroid placement.
reviews.detail: §IV-A states the exception. The impossibility proof is conditional on identical nonoverlapping single-site units, not arbitrary nested device geometry.

reviews.detail: §IV-C specifies placement exceptions and separate top-plate routing.

reviews.original_attached_text: Neighboring units of a capacitor become connected components found by breadth-first search. Bottom-plate branch wires connect units, vertical trunks connect components, and peripheral bridges join trunks. Each symmetric connection is mirrored. Separate top-plate routing uses a graph/MST to connect electrically common plates while minimizing added top-to-substrate capacitance. In a split DAC the LSB and MSB top-plate graphs remain separate except for the attenuation capacitor. §IV-B–C, PDF pp. 8–10
reviews.supported_claim: Same-bit connected components use branches/trunks/bridges; common top plates use graph/MST routing, separately for split banks.
reviews.detail: §IV-B and §IV-C checked. MST is a construction heuristic under its graph cost, not an optimal electrical-delay proof.

reviews.original_attached_text: The authors use parallel wires to reduce resistance on critical bits while respecting discrete wire widths. A widened or parallel-routed critical bit can cause a different bit to become the slowest; therefore repeat the all-bit delay evaluation after every improvement. More parallel routes eventually add enough capacitance and channel demand to give diminishing returns. Results and Fig. 15, PDF pp. 11–12
reviews.supported_claim: Parallel wiring can reduce delay, change the critical bit and reach diminishing returns.
reviews.detail: Tables I–II and Fig.15/discussion checked. Benefits are limited to the paper’s RC/via/route model.

reviews.original_attached_text: Equations (17)–(18) define code-step DNL and ideal-transfer INL in LSB units. Preserve their reference convention: endpoint-fitted or best-fit INL removes different errors. For an N-bit transfer with codes 0…2 N −1 there are 2 N −1 adjacent transitions. Report the worst code and transition, not just an array-level average. §III, PDF p. 4
reviews.supported_claim: DNL uses adjacent code steps and INL uses a stated ideal transfer reference in LSB units.
reviews.detail: Eqs.(17)–(18) checked. Endpoint/best-fit convention discussion is handbook clarification; the 3-bit example is derived with explicit nominal reference and no gain removal.

reviews.original_attached_text: The authors label this a 3-dB frequency, but its N-dependent expression is tied to their charge/discharge settling model. It is not interchangeable with the sinusoidal −3 dB pole of a first-order RC, 1/(2πτ) . Philis should name the reported metric explicitly and validate transient settling to a stated LSB error. This distinction is our interpretation of the displayed equation, visually checked in the PDF. §III-C and Eq. (32), PDF pp. 5–6
reviews.supported_claim: The paper defines f=1/[2(N+2)ln(2)τ], with τ from charging-path delay.
reviews.detail: Eq.(32) was visually checked. The handbook distinguishes this N-dependent settling model from a standard single-pole −3 dB frequency; this is a dimensional/model interpretation, not a publisher erratum.

reviews.original_attached_text: For the nonunit MOM bridge capacitor, the paper derives an effective perimeter/area-like condition. With coupling length l and height H, its small edge-shift model gives ΔC/C≈2δ(1/H+1/l) . Matching this quantity to the unit capacitor while solving for target capacitance gives two geometric equations. The result assumes the paper's MOM construction, small common edge shifts, and continuous dimensions; legal pitch quantization and fringe effects require extraction afterward. §III-D, PDF p. 6
reviews.supported_claim: For the paper’s MOM bridge construction and common small edge shift, ΔC/C≈2δ(1/H+1/l).
reviews.detail: §III-D Eqs.(39)–(45) checked. H is the planar finger-array height, not dielectric thickness. Continuous dimensions and small common perturbation are required.

reviews.original_attached_text: The reported experiments show a real tradeoff: spiral layouts favor the modeled frequency, chessboard layouts favor dispersion/linearity, and block chessboards occupy intermediate points. Table II's 8-bit examples, for instance, give about 1411 MHz for spiral and 339 MHz for block chessboard under the paper's frequency model, with different INL/DNL. These values are evidence for the mechanism in that setup, not Philis performance targets. Tables I–II, PDF p. 11
reviews.supported_claim: Table II lists roughly 1411 MHz spiral versus 339 MHz block chessboard for the 8-bit example.
reviews.detail: Dense table values were checked in raster. These use the paper’s frequency model and experimental assumptions; no engine benchmark is claimed.

reviews.original_attached_text: The paper itself warns that its commonly reused gradient and correlation parameters are inherited from earlier work and are not a measured capacitor correlation characterization. This is an especially valuable methodological result: do not turn ρ=0.9 , a 1 mm correlation length, or a 10 ppm gradient into default manufacturing truth. Sweep uncertain values and label them assumed until the PDK or measurements justify them. Parameter discussion, PDF p. 12
reviews.supported_claim: The commonly reused gradient/correlation constants are assumed rather than measured capacitor-process characterization.
reviews.detail: §V setup and parameter discussion explicitly disclose inherited parameters. Joint-yield objections to separate marginal 3σ substitutions are handbook statistical interpretation.

reviews.original_attached_text: The general covariance form, useful for an engine implementation, is σ² e ≈ J C J T . This matrix expression is a proposed generalization of the paper's independent-parameter equation. Correlations must either be retained or represented by a justified independent parameter basis; they must not disappear merely because a data structure stores independent coefficients. The paper evaluates sensitivities using the compact transistor model in SPICE, thereby including weak and strong inversion, linear and saturation operation, body bias, series resistance, and short/narrow/graded-channel behavior represented by that model. Accuracy is still limited by the compact model, measured data and linearization. Eqs. (7)–(11), PDF p. 3 .
reviews.supported_claim: Independent-parameter first-order propagation of variance, evaluated with compact-model sensitivities.
reviews.detail: Eq. (8) supplies the independent case. J C J^T is the handbook covariance derivation, now explicitly labeled as such instead of calling it a proposed paper expression.

reviews.original_label: Parameter distinction and Eq. (6), PDF p. 2
reviews.original_attached_text: Threshold voltage depends on oxide thickness, doping, geometry and several short/narrow-channel effects. β shares physical dependencies, including oxide thickness. Treating the two as independent random causes can count the same physical fluctuation twice. The paper reports that such double counting can produce substantial prediction error. Likewise, a threshold mismatch number is not generally an input offset number: the local input-referred relation is σ Vgs = σ Id /g m , and both current mismatch and g m vary with bias. An input pair's performance must therefore be evaluated where it operates. Parameter distinction and Eq. (6), PDF p. 2 .
reviews.supported_claim: Threshold/current-factor parameter dependencies can double count oxide-thickness variation; current mismatch maps locally to input-referred voltage through transconductance.
reviews.detail: Visually checked Table I and Eq. (6). Notes now explicitly require absolute current standard deviation in amperes before division by gm; relative current variation needs multiplication by nominal current.

reviews.original_attached_text: Back propagation of variance fits physical-parameter variances to measured electrical mismatch using a matrix of squared compact-model sensitivities. Measurements must span geometries and biases that make each parameter observable. For example, source/drain sheet resistance becomes visible under conditions where channel resistance is relatively small; a dataset consisting only of extracted threshold values cannot identify it. The resulting regression is useful only when the parameter set is identifiable above measurement error. The paper distinguishes this physics-based parameterization from an empirical principal-component fit. Back propagation and observability, PDF p. 3 .

reviews.original_attached_text: A route is a manufactured, heated conductor carrying a time-dependent current through a particular geometry. Its reliability depends on every narrow section, bend, pin access, via, material boundary, and operating condition. A connected route with legal minimum widths can still fail. The central lesson of Jens Lienig and Matthias Thiele’s Fundamentals of Electromigration-Aware Integrated Circuit Design (2018) is to make these electrical and reliability requirements inputs to construction, not merely checks after routing. An optimal route minimizes its area, parasitics, and routing obstruction subject to a stated service life and failure probability under its mission profile. Chapter 3 ; constraint-driven design, chapter 5 .
reviews.supported_claim: Reliability-aware physical construction needs current constraints and may use a library of preverified routing elements.
reviews.detail: Chapter 3 introduction and §§5.3,5.5 support the physical-design direction. The particular Philis architecture is a proposal, not an implementation reported by these authors.

reviews.original_attached_text: Electron momentum transfer drives metal atoms along available diffusion paths. Uniform material flow through an ideal uniform conductor does not alone identify the point of damage: accumulation and depletion arise where the flux diverges. Geometric necks, interfaces, grain boundaries, temperature gradients, and blocked ends change that flow. Depletion produces voids and resistance increase; accumulation can produce extrusions and shorts. The first electrical consequence can therefore be degraded gain, bias, settling, or supply regulation before an open circuit appears. A progressively smaller conducting cross-section raises current density and heating, creating positive feedback. Physical mechanisms, PDF 25–33 .
reviews.supported_claim: Nonuniform atomic flux causes depletion/accumulation and electrical degradation, with current-density and heating feedback.
reviews.detail: Source explains voids, hillocks, resistance change, flux divergence and feedback. Analog gain/offset examples in notes are explicit circuit consequences, not measured source benchmarks.

reviews.original_attached_text: Three coupled transport mechanisms matter. Electromigration follows the electrical driving force; thermomigration follows a temperature gradient; stress migration responds to mechanical stress gradients. Stress induced by atom accumulation can oppose EM and help a confined wire, but thermal-expansion mismatch, manufacturing stress, and an unfavorable package or neighboring heater can introduce different stress gradients. A router must distinguish helpful back stress from externally imposed stress rather than assign a generic “stress bonus.” Thermal and stress migration, PDF 45–57 .
reviews.supported_claim: Diffusion depends on material interfaces; thermal and mechanical migration interact with electrical migration.
reviews.detail: Checked §§2.3.1,2.4.2,2.4.4,2.5 and 4.8. Separate back stress from external stress, and process-specific material behavior from universal constants. Relevant coupled fluxes are Eqs. (2.15)–(2.18), PDF54–55. Thermal chapter adds derived circuit implications.

reviews.original_attached_text: Diffusion paths depend on the manufactured stack. Grain boundaries are particularly relevant in aluminum; copper surface and interface diffusion can dominate despite copper’s better conductivity. Liners, dielectric caps, dielectric stiffness, CMP damage, and grain structure alter the governing mechanism. A nominal metal name is consequently insufficient to transfer an activation energy between processes. Process development can change materials; a layout engine generally chooses among the stack and primitives the foundry actually supplies. Diffusion mechanisms ; materials and boundaries .

reviews.original_attached_text: The second expression is the generalized Black relation. The book presents a median failure time, not a guarantee that every wire survives. Its coefficient, activation energy, and current exponent must describe the process, geometry, failure criterion, and dominant failure mechanism. A fitted exponent near one for growth-limited failure and near two for nucleation-limited failure is an observation discussed by the book, not permission to select either value without calibration. Extrapolating accelerated testing across a mechanism change is particularly risky. Black’s relation and limitations, PDF 30–33 .
reviews.supported_claim: Generalized Black equation models calibrated median time to failure and has process/geometry/failure-mechanism limitations.
reviews.detail: Verified Eq. (2.1), its exponent generalization, and Eq. (3.8). Notes correctly use median, not a guarantee or a mean lifetime. Fixed-lifetime temperature scaling is derived separately.

reviews.original_label: Mission profiles and failure probability, PDF 91–98
reviews.original_attached_text: A circuit contains many vulnerable locations. A median lifetime for one test structure is not the allowed failure probability for the entire product. The analysis needs the distribution of lifetimes, characterization confidence, target percentile, total exposure, and allocation of reliability among features. The book’s mission-profile treatment connects manufacturing, storage, and operating modes with time, temperature, and current. Reusing a route under a new operating profile invalidates the old reliability claim unless the profile remains inside the characterized envelope. Mission profiles and failure probability, PDF 91–98 .
reviews.supported_claim: Mission profile, characterization confidence, target lifetime, and failure quantile are needed in addition to a single wire median lifetime.
reviews.detail: Checked §§3.4.1–3.4.2. Notes avoid reproducing the more questionable scaling expressions in the book and do not assert independent wire failures or unqualified linear damage accumulation.

reviews.original_attached_text: A single operating-point current is inadequate for a switched bias, output stage, clock buffer, or charging capacitor. Mean signed current describes directional transport only within an appropriate recovery model. RMS current controls resistive heating for a fixed resistance. Peak current constrains short-pulse and electrical-overstress behavior under separate pulse rules. All three may determine dimensions, and the largest applicable requirement governs. Current reversals can partially undo directional transport, but zero signed average does not imply zero heating or infinite life. Unequal positive and negative pulses, material boundaries, nonlinear diffusion, and thermal time constants can defeat simplistic cancellation. Alternating-current effects ; current classification, PDF 82–86 .
reviews.supported_claim: RMS, directional/equivalent average, peak, and waveform/frequency classes serve different reliability mechanisms; reversal does not guarantee immortality.
reviews.detail: Checked §§2.4.3,3.3.1,4.7 and summary. Notes deliberately do not universalize the book’s differing numerical frequency thresholds. RMS is a heating metric for fixed resistance, with recovery needing characterization.

reviews.original_attached_text: The book uses frequency thresholds to organize example flows. Those thresholds are not universal material constants. Whether a pulse behaves as DC stress, recoverable alternating stress, or a separate transient event depends on the process and waveform. Its minimum-feature digital-wire skin-effect discussion also does not eliminate RF loss analysis for wider top metal, inductors, or high-frequency analog structures. Frequency effects, PDF 140–142 and 154 .
reviews.supported_claim: RMS, directional/equivalent average, peak, and waveform/frequency classes serve different reliability mechanisms; reversal does not guarantee immortality.
reviews.detail: Checked §§2.4.3,3.3.1,4.7 and summary. Notes deliberately do not universalize the book’s differing numerical frequency thresholds. RMS is a heating metric for fixed resistance, with recovery needing characterization.

reviews.original_attached_text: At a terminal, current has direction as well as magnitude. A multi-terminal net may contain sources and sinks that change roles during operation. A scalar maximum absolute current at each terminal loses phase and cancellation information and cannot, in general, determine the worst current in a Steiner branch. The book constructs signed lower and upper terminal-current bounds and derives branch demands from topology. For a tree, cutting an edge separates the terminals into two sets; the branch current equals the signed sum on either side, with consistent orientation. For a resistive mesh, current sharing requires a network solution. Terminal currents and topology, PDF 83–90 .
reviews.supported_claim: Segment demand depends on signed terminal currents, modes, waveform relations, and tree topology.
reviews.detail: Checked Eqs. (3.1)–(3.7), Figs. 3.4–3.10. Notes preserve temporal correlation rather than assert independent maxima occur together. Added omitted condition: include interconnect shunt/displacement currents as loads, or state that they are neglected, before using a cut-sum identity.

reviews.original_attached_text: Topology and wire dimensions are coupled. The shortest-length tree can leave a long branch carrying the sum of many loads, requiring a wide trunk and more capacitance. A current-aware objective can minimize Σ length × required width, subject to voltage drop, parasitic, and congestion limits. Reconnecting one load changes upstream currents; therefore branch annotations must be invalidated and recomputed after topology changes. Current-driven topology construction .
reviews.supported_claim: Current-aware wire planning minimizes required metal area rather than only geometric wire length.
reviews.detail: Old PDF87 anchor was the segment-current derivation. Changed to PDF90, §3.3.3 and Fig. 3.10, where the area objective and topology/current circular dependency are explicitly discussed.

reviews.original_attached_text: The book’s sizing flow takes the maximum dimension required by equivalent-current, peak-current, and manufacturing rules, then accounts for process-dependent cross-section loss. The same reasoning must include bends, necks, contacts, and device-access metal. A wide global wire connected through a narrow pin throat does not have the capacity of its widest segment. Landing location on a complex pin changes the internal current path; pin accessibility is therefore an electrical property as well as a geometrical one. Dimensioning and pin accessibility, PDF 99–105 .
reviews.supported_claim: Dimensioning must combine current types, manufacturing cross-section corrections, and pin-access ampacity.
reviews.detail: Verified Eqs. (3.21)–(3.24), Fig.3.15, §§3.5.2–3.5.5. Corrected the term volumetric current density to cross-sectional current density for A/cm². Illustrative density and width arithmetic checked independently.

reviews.original_attached_text: Via redundancy improves manufacturing connectivity and can improve reliability, but dividing total current by the number of cuts assumes equal sharing. At an orthogonal layer transition, inner cuts can have shorter, lower-resistance access paths and carry more current than outer cuts. Simply adding distant cuts may barely relieve the hottest one. The book illustrates this with spatial current-density solutions and arrangements that equalize access path lengths. Adjacent metal geometry and allowed directional routing determine whether such an arrangement is useful in a real deck. Multiple vias, PDF 134–140 .
reviews.supported_claim: Via redundancy does not guarantee equal current sharing; access geometry, current direction and reservoirs matter.
reviews.detail: Checked §§4.6.1–4.6.5 and Figs.4.25–4.29; source figures support the conceptual SVG. The warm-colored drawing is clearly not a field simulation. Four-cut worked example checked as conditional on its assumed crowding factor.

reviews.original_attached_text: In PDF page 101, printed equations 3.25–3.26 multiply the required via count by a factor that decreases when the application temperature rises above the reference temperature. The page was visually inspected; this is not merely text-extraction corruption. Under fixed-lifetime Black scaling with positive activation energy, that decreasing factor describes allowable current , whose inverse is needed when determining the number of equally loaded vias. Before implementing those printed equations, resolve the convention against the foundry model. The physically consistent fixed-lifetime relation derived from Black’s expression is j allow (T)/j allow (T ref ) = exp[(E a /nk)(1/T − 1/T ref )]. Higher temperature decreases allowable current. A required-width/count implementation needs a monotonicity test that catches the opposite result. The supplied equations .
reviews.supported_claim: Printed Eqs.3.25–3.26 produce a required-via-count factor with the opposite temperature monotonicity to fixed-lifetime Black current scaling.
reviews.detail: Independently inspected the rendered PDF101, printed p89. Eq3.25 multiplies count by f and Eq3.26 gives f<1 when Teff>Tref. Re-derived allowable current ratio from Eq3.8. Retain as apparent internal inconsistency, not a verified publisher erratum or a foundry-qualified replacement rule.

reviews.original_attached_text: In a sufficiently confined conductor, EM creates a stress gradient that drives atoms back. Balancing the two driving forces gives a critical current-density–length product of the form |jL| crit = ΩΔσ/(e|Z*|ρ). The symbols represent atomic volume, allowed stress difference, effective charge, and resistivity. The length is a physical diffusion domain under the model’s boundary conditions. It is not the distance between arbitrary routing vertices. Inserting a software node does not create a diffusion barrier. Blech effect, PDF 117–127 .
reviews.supported_claim: The Blech product is a conditional one-dimensional stress-balance criterion, with distinct void-nucleation and growth-saturation limits.
reviews.detail: Verified Eq.(4.1), Eq.(4.2) discussion, simple-segment limitation PDF123, transient caveat PDF127, and neighboring-segment/reservoir interaction PDF130. Notes correctly refuse to make a software vertex into a diffusion barrier. Added e and dimensionless Z* definitions.

reviews.original_attached_text: Via-above and via-below configurations in dual-Damascene stacks can tolerate different void volumes before losing electrical connection. The direction and landing layer consequently matter. Reservoir metal can supply atoms at one boundary yet weaken helpful stress buildup at another; current reversal can exchange those roles. Bamboo grains can suppress one diffusion path while narrowing the wire raises resistance and heating, and copper interface diffusion may remain dominant. These are candidate techniques enabled by a qualified process model, not independent boolean optimizations. Bamboo limitations ; via orientation and reservoirs, PDF 127–133 .
reviews.supported_claim: Bamboo structures suppress suitable grain-boundary diffusion but require process/material conditions and may lose benefit to self-heating or interface diffusion.
reviews.detail: Verified §4.2 and Fig.4.1. The notes correctly avoid claiming the aluminum result transfers directly to ordinary copper.

reviews.original_attached_text: The material chapters explain why dielectric stiffness, caps, liners, and copper interfaces affect back stress and activation energy. Carbon nanotubes and composites are research directions discussed in the 2018 source, with explicit contact, integration, and thermal limitations. Their theoretical current densities cannot be substituted into a conventional CMOS routing deck. The useful architectural lesson is to keep material and primitive capabilities extensible. Material stack and alternatives, PDF 142–154 .

reviews.detail: Notes present the 2018 outlook as historical research scope and do not claim present-day PDK availability or use tabulated material values as foundry limits.

reviews.original_attached_text: Current density follows the electrical potential solution and conductivity. Local finite-element or resistance-mesh models expose crowding that average width rules miss. Electrothermal analysis updates resistivity and temperature together; stress and atom-transport analysis adds further state for reliability prediction. The mesh and geometric representation require convergence checks: a mathematical sharp corner can create a singular result, but indiscriminately smoothing it can erase a real manufactured neck. Use actual process geometry and a characterized local criterion. Numerical modeling, PDF 58–69 ; current-density verification .
reviews.supported_claim: Analytical, lumped and meshed approaches trade cost against spatial fidelity; coupled boundaries and template interfaces must be respected.
reviews.detail: Checked §2.6.1 and §§3.5.4–3.5.5. Numerical method descriptions are supported; thermal PDE/RC equations in handbook are energy-conservation/Fourier-law derivations, not equations asserted to appear in this EM passage. New precise Hastings citations support the thermal basis.

reviews.original_attached_text: A full multiphysics solve during every routing move is impractical. The book proposes precharacterized reliable routing elements, such as straight sections, bends, transitions, and via arrays. Such a library is especially applicable to Philis: annotate a legal template with current, temperature, direction, and boundary ranges; reject use outside those ranges; and verify the interactions when templates are joined. Individually valid blocks do not automatically compose if adjoining blocks change thermal conditions, stress reservoirs, current direction, or access geometry. Routing-element library, PDF 165–167 .
reviews.supported_claim: A technology-qualified routing-element library can reduce verification cost, but joined-element interactions still need checking.
reviews.detail: §5.3 explicitly requires mutual-interaction examination after composition; §2.6.1 demonstrates distinct versus combined FEM patterns. Notes preserve this caveat.

reviews.original_attached_text: Source finding. The text repeatedly trades area against precision, compactness against local interactions, shielding against other physical effects, and device size against parasitic load. Its chapter 8 discussion explicitly explains that adding more sections to a fixed-area array can reduce gradient error while increasing random mismatch because spacing consumes active area. It also states that a CC arrangement offers no matching benefit if the relevant gradients are absent. PDF pp. 392–394
reviews.supported_claim: Common-centroid refinement trades gradient suppression against lost active area and implementation cost
reviews.detail: Original label said pp392–394 but hyperlink opened393; changed anchor to392.

reviews.original_attached_text: Chapters 1–4 explain why shapes on different layers are not interchangeable obstacles. Diffusion extends beyond the drawn opening; depletion extends beyond the metallurgical junction; implanted dopants have tails; oxide steps alter topography; local pattern density alters printing, etching, or polishing; contacts and vias depend on the actual metal process. Minimum dimensions include manufacturing tolerances and electrical requirements. Consequently, a device footprint alone cannot express all interactions. PDF pp. 79–95 , 138–144
reviews.supported_claim: Lithography, diffusion, implantation and etching create dimensions and surroundings that differ from drawn rectangles
reviews.detail: Original span did not cover the contact/interconnect/CMP clauses. Added §2.7 PDF99–110; original span remains appropriate for front-end process mechanisms.

reviews.original_attached_text: Source finding. Random variation, systematic dimensional bias, neighboring-pattern effects, contact/interconnect resistance, temperature, stress and electric fields are distinct mechanisms. Increasing active area averages some random fluctuations; it does not automatically remove systematic error. The simpler inverse-square-root-of-area relation is an approximation when areal variation dominates peripheral variation. The book also distinguishes absolute accuracy from ratio matching and from resolution. PDF pp. 368–375 , 418
reviews.supported_claim: Random variation, systematic biases, proximity and interconnect terms must not be collapsed into a single area law
reviews.detail: Inverse-square-root area law is an areal-dominance approximation. Source includes peripheral contributions and process-specific coefficients.

The coefficient is obtained from measurements. The text explicitly cautions against overtrusting its oxide-thickness rule of thumb, discusses backgate-bias dependence, and gives exceptions involving small geometries and pocket implants. That is evidence for storing a mismatch model per device family and operating regime, not treating one dimensionless ratio of gradient to random error as universal. PDF pp. 687–690

reviews.detail: Long-channel strong-inversion formulas are scoped approximations; minimum-size/short-channel behavior is not inferred from them.

reviews.original_attached_text: Coincident centroids cancel a linear spatial contribution under the assumptions behind that averaging. They do not cancel all higher-order variation, local discontinuities, arbitrary coupling, or different terminal voltages. Hastings' four passive-device rules are coincidence, symmetry, subdivision into smaller common-centroid groups, and compactness; MOS devices add orientation. The revised third-edition notion of dispersion specifically favors repeatable small balanced subarrays over merely spreading labels uniformly. PDF pp. 392–394 , 709–711

reviews.detail: Source does not claim that every fine interdigitation cancels nonlinear gradients or that CC helps without a meaningful gradient.

reviews.original_attached_text: Chapter 6 shows why a resistor is not just sheet resistance multiplied by drawn length/width. It has dimension biases, contact crowding, end effects, corner effects, nonlinear voltage and temperature dependence, distributed capacitance, and sometimes parasitic junctions. For a right-angle equal-width corner, the book gives 0.5587 squares rather than the approximate half-square mnemonic. This small difference matters if the algorithm uses many corners to obtain a precision ratio. Dogbone heads do not inherently make two devices match better: identical systematic head contributions can cancel, while unmatched heads cannot. PDF pp. 279–295
reviews.supported_claim: Effective resistor geometry includes width/length bias, contact/end terms, corners and conductivity modulation
reviews.detail: Eq6.10 gives 0.5587 squares for its ideal equal-width right-angle corner; not a process-independent corner model. Notes correctly distinguish identical-head cancellation from absolute error.

reviews.original_attached_text: Equation 8.34 is E T = S ΔT C , where S is the contact Seebeck coefficient and ΔT C is the temperature difference between a segment's contacts. Figure 8.22, visually checked here, contrasts connections that add these voltages with connections that largely cancel them. The engine should trace the ordered path through each series chain and accumulate signed thermoelectric sources. This is separate from matching the average resistance under a temperature field. Close placement of serpentine heads reduces endpoint temperature difference, but their orientation must also address mask-alignment sensitivity. PDF pp. 401–402
reviews.supported_claim: Contact-temperature differences produce signed thermoelectric voltages that common-centroid placement alone cannot cancel
reviews.detail: Visually checked Eq8.34 and Fig8.22; cancellation depends on connection direction and matched temperature drops, not merely even segment count.

reviews.original_attached_text: Material and trim decisions. Thin-film, poly, diffusion, well, metal and pinched resistors occupy different places in the accuracy/area/power/parasitic trade space. Diffused resistors can dissipate heat more effectively through silicon, while deposited resistors avoid the same junction parasitics. Trimming can compensate a value at its calibration condition, but cannot generally remove thermal gradients, material-dependent temperature behavior, hysteresis or later drift. Preserve trim accessibility, programming-current paths and exclusions when trim structures are present; component substitution or adding trim is a circuit-design choice, not a permissible placement repair. PDF pp. 295–323 , 418–422
reviews.supported_claim: Resistor materials and trimming methods trade area, parasitics, power and stability
reviews.detail: Checked relevant material/trim passages. A single-condition trim cannot generally remove other independent environmental errors; that limiting statement is synthesis, not a quoted universal source theorem.

reviews.original_attached_text: Vertical bipolar devices. Match emitter geometry and use identical unit emitters for ratios. Active emitter area and perimeter determine injection, while base resistance, base/emitter contacts, collector resistance, Early effect and saturation alter the terminal currents. Compact clusters and common-centroid arrays help with temperature and stress fields, but contact and base distributions also need balancing. Placing collector contacts outside an array can bring its critical emitters closer together. When emitters share a base, do not blindly exploit the smaller “connected-emitter” spacing: overlapping depletion regions can alter carrier flow even when the terminals share a net. PDF pp. 506–526
reviews.supported_claim: BJT random/systematic matching depends on emitter geometry, current density, bias, thermal environment and connection effects
reviews.detail: Matched unit construction and cautions are source-backed. Numerical thermal and beta examples are explicitly hypothetical circuit derivations.

reviews.original_attached_text: Lateral bipolar devices. Both emitter and collector geometry matter because current flows laterally between them. A larger single emitter can reduce current gain, so the source often favors arrays of small emitters rather than simply enlarging one device. Match the collector's inner perimeter, base/contact environment and applicable field plates. A saturated collector can reinject carriers into neighboring collectors; equal nominal base nets do not make shared tanks harmless. Separate isolation regions can be worth their area where collector efficiency or saturation threatens matching. PDF pp. 527–529
reviews.supported_claim: Lateral BJT perimeter, collector arrangement and field environment differ from vertical-emitter area scaling
reviews.detail: A larger emitter is not automatically a better lateral PNP; the notes preserve the device-family distinction.

reviews.original_attached_text: Operating-point limits. Keep precision bipolar devices in their characterized current-density range, below problematic high-level injection and away from low-current leakage/recombination dominance. Equalize collector voltages when the circuit requires suppression of Early-effect error. Emitter degeneration transfers sensitivity from a transistor to a resistor and costs voltage headroom; it is an architectural option, not something the placer can add. Guard against reverse emitter-base stress, which can degrade current gain before an obvious catastrophic failure. A ratioed bandgap pair also relies on accurate temperature tracking; a common centroid does not remove all nonlinear thermal behavior. PDF pp. 509–523 , 526
reviews.supported_claim: Thermal and terminal/beta effects can turn a nominal current ratio into a VBE error
reviews.detail: Checked bias/temperature mechanisms and independently recomputed the 8:1, 1%, beta-ratio and 50mK examples. No example temperature coefficient is represented as universal.

reviews.original_attached_text: PN diodes. Diode-connected transistors inherit their parent family’s matching limitations. Control the actual regulated current: emitter-current regulation includes base current, so it is not identical to collector-current regulation. Match junction shape, contact arrangement, guard structures, material and surrounding diffusions. Distinguish series resistance from junction-voltage error and include leakage over temperature. PDF pp. 565–571
reviews.supported_claim: PN, Schottky and Zener matching cannot share a single generic diode objective
reviews.detail: Source distinguishes emitter versus collector current and nonuniform avalanche conduction.

reviews.original_attached_text: Zeners. Localized avalanche can let one region with the lowest breakdown voltage dominate the entire junction. Consequently, increasing area does not generally deliver inverse-square-root matching at low current. Surface walkout/walkback and unequal accumulated charge can produce later divergence. Use a characterized structure and lifecycle model; neither a circular outline nor CC placement can promise precise Zener matching. PDF pp. 566–567
reviews.supported_claim: Paralleled Zener segments can share avalanche current nonuniformly rather than average like ordinary passive units
reviews.detail: Source mechanism checked; no Pelgrom-style universal Zener improvement is claimed.

reviews.original_attached_text: Schottky diodes. Barrier material, inhomogeneity, contact perimeter, field relief and series resistance matter. A guard ring can improve field uniformity but can also inject minority carriers when it forward biases. The source's comparison of aluminum and noble-silicide Schottkies demonstrates why material-specific primitives are necessary; it is not a license to synthesize an unqualified barrier. PDF pp. 568–571
reviews.supported_claim: Schottky material/barrier/contact/field geometry and guard-junction bias affect leakage, voltage and minority injection
reviews.detail: Added §11.2 PDF563 to directly support the forward-biased field-relief guard-junction injection clause. Original matching span alone was incomplete.

reviews.original_attached_text: Integrated inductors. More turns do not monotonically improve performance. Winding resistance, skin/proximity effects, substrate eddy currents and parasitic capacitance compete with inductance and mutual coupling. High frequency makes conductor shape, neighboring metal and return paths part of the device. The source favors high-level, low-resistance metal, short leads, a controlled empty center and limited unrelated material nearby. A solid shield can create eddy-current loss; a patterned shield must interrupt the relevant current loops. Stacking metal in parallel is different from adding serial winding layers, which can greatly increase interwinding capacitance. PDF pp. 355–363
reviews.supported_claim: Inductor performance depends on winding resistance, frequency effects, substrate/metal surroundings, shielding and parasitic capacitance
reviews.detail: §7.2.1–2 supports EM-environment constraints. Q≈ωL/R and the ideal LC resonance example are stated as simplified circuit estimates, not as a universal extracted model.

reviews.original_attached_text: Power bipolar devices. Emitter debiasing, thermal runaway and turnoff current focusing distinguish continuous, switching and pulsed operation. Base contact placement and ballast must be designed for those conditions. A structure good for a linear pass element can have poor reverse-bias safe operating area during turnoff. Repeating a small-signal transistor until its total area is large enough does not establish power capability. PDF pp. 485–505
reviews.supported_claim: Power bipolar devices require debiasing, ballast and electrothermal/SOA analysis appropriate to their switching regime
reviews.detail: Checked central power-device mechanisms. Broad source span also covers detailed structures not reproduced in notes.

reviews.original_attached_text: Power MOS devices. Include silicon, metal and package contributions to on-resistance. Limit distributed gate delay, keep source/body resistance under control, and check electrical as well as electrothermal safe operating area. A positive temperature coefficient in some operating regions does not imply universal immunity to current localization: the text discusses impact-ionization feedback and the Spirito effect. SenseFET units must sample comparable temperature, terminal voltage and edge environments; a small sense element at the edge can see first-finger effects absent from the average main transistor. PDF pp. 644–668
reviews.supported_claim: MOS power layouts combine silicon/metal/package R, distributed gate delay, body resistance, SOA and SenseFET environment
reviews.detail: Source-backed mechanism survey. The approximate distributed-finger equation is separately audited; SenseFET pattern proposals require extraction and bias/thermal equivalence.

reviews.original_attached_text: For a uniformly distributed, singly terminated metal finger, the source derives an effective added resistance approximately one third of its disconnected end-to-end resistance. That differs from a lead delivering all its current to a load at the far end: current is collected or delivered continuously along the finger. Unequal material coverage, tapering or strong debiasing requires a fuller distributed model. PDF pp. 650–664 , 870–876

reviews.original_attached_text: Antenna is fabrication-history dependent. A long conductor may not yet connect to a gate when its layer is etched. Conversely, a small final connected component can have a problematic exposure history. The book distinguishes areal and peripheral ratios and discusses latent connections during incomplete etching. A higher-layer jumper changes the earlier connected component; it is not merely a change in final total wire area. A top-layer violation cannot be repaired by jumping to a nonexistent higher layer. A diode brings junction capacitance, leakage, placement and sometimes illumination requirements, all of which must be checked. PDF pp. 228–230

reviews.original_attached_text: ESD protection must remain benign during operation. A snapback clamp has trigger and holding behavior, while a rate-triggered device responds to slew. A normal power-up ramp, a failsafe input above an unpowered supply, or an external source able to sustain holding current can therefore alter device choice. Extra rail width alone cannot repair a clamp that is inappropriate for the application. Primary pad protection also does not ensure a nearby thin gate survives fast local discharge; return points and local secondary clamps matter. The book's illustrated HBM/CDM values are examples from specific structures and eras, not current universal qualification requirements. PDF pp. 749–752 , 766–776
reviews.supported_claim: Clipping, snapback and rate-triggered primary protection have different allowed-operation and secondary-protection requirements
reviews.detail: Local protected terminals/reference and intentional limiting impedance must be preserved.

reviews.original_attached_text: A substrate tap usually reduces majority-carrier voltage drop. A minority-carrier collecting ring intercepts carriers at a suitable reverse-biased junction. A blocking ring uses an effective high-low junction or dielectric barrier to obstruct their path. These are different mechanisms even when their top views look like similar rings. The relevant carrier type, depth, buried layer, bias and contact resistance determine whether carriers pass beneath a ring, over a weak junction, or through an opening. PDF pp. 256–270 , 735–742

reviews.original_attached_text: Sharing is an electrical transformation. Merging devices in a common well/tank saves repeated isolation area but introduces shared resistance, junction capacitance and minority-carrier paths. Net equivalence is necessary for many mergers but not sufficient for safe operation. Saturating lateral PNPs, noisy isolated MOS devices, shared contacts carrying large current, and resistors whose bodies become forward biased illustrate the failure modes. Whitelist qualified merger templates with terminal/bias and injection conditions, and otherwise retain separate regions. A merge should be re-extracted and rechecked under scenarios, not approved merely because DRC and nominal LVS pass. PDF pp. 723–734 , 600
reviews.supported_claim: Device sharing can introduce minority-carrier injection, common-resistance debiasing and capacitively mediated errors
reviews.detail: Whitelist/re-extract transformation procedure is original synthesis. The source supports why schematic net equality alone is insufficient.

reviews.original_attached_text: Kelvin and star connections. The physical point at which sense and force conductors join determines which voltage drop the circuit measures. If they merge before the intended device or pad, shared current creates an unwanted offset. Separate net names and schematic resistors can assist LVS but do not prove the junction is in the right physical location. Likewise, matched emitters or sources should join an intended star at the actual location where common-mode rather than differential IR drop is desired. Include finite sense current and lead resistance for high accuracy. PDF p. 818
reviews.supported_claim: A Kelvin/star connection must join physically at the intended reference; sharing a net name does not remove IR drop
reviews.detail: Read Figures15.26–15.27 and text; finite sense current and common path matter.

reviews.original_attached_text: Noise. Coupling depends on aggressor slew, coupling capacitance, victim impedance and timing, not merely the aggressor's average frequency. A configuration bit that switches infrequently can still upset a sensitive measurement. Use circuit roles to separate incompatible nets, controlled crossing geometry, and shields tied to the relevant quiet reference. Check the shield's impedance; a shared noisy return can defeat its purpose. Slowing a signal is a possible circuit-level remedy only when its timing permits it. PDF pp. 819–820
reviews.supported_claim: Capacitive coupling depends on slew and victim impedance; shielding requires a suitable low-impedance reference
reviews.detail: Eq15.23 is an illustrative lumped relation. Notes do not promise that a shield removes all coupling or that a logically static net has no startup transitions.

reviews.original_attached_text: Voltage and current. High-voltage spacing depends on the maximum voltage difference between adjacent conductors under allowed scenarios, not just their voltage to ground. EM is a local bottleneck condition; resistance is an integrated path quantity. The source's via illustration shows why vias near the inside of a corner carry more current than nominally identical outer vias. Prefer appropriate straight transitions and sufficient distributed access, then check the actual current distribution. PDF pp. 821–822
reviews.supported_claim: Local neck/via current density can dominate reliability although total resistance integrates along the path
reviews.detail: Visually checked Fig15.29. An inside-corner via array does not share current uniformly; straight transitions reduce the illustrated nonuniformity.

reviews.original_attached_text: Capacity and access. Route pitch must account for via footprint, enclosure and output-grid legality, not only minimum line spacing. Reserve space for wide supplies, shields, matched routes and local access before filling channels with ordinary signals. At intersecting channels, available tracks can disappear into turning and via demand; a channel-width scalar alone is an imperfect congestion model. Use blockage/access-aware estimation early enough to revise the floorplan. PDF pp. 811–817
reviews.supported_claim: Real routability depends on layer direction, via enclosure, pitch, grid and channel junction capacity
reviews.detail: Not all via families stack legally. Worked 100+100 pitch versus140 landing example is explicit arithmetic under hypothetical dimensions.

reviews.original_attached_text: Thermal and stress placement. Conventional molded-package stress often has low gradients near the die center despite large absolute stress there. Heat-source avoidance can favor an off-center location. Bumps, pillars, die attach, board loading and multiple changing power sources create different distributions. Optimize the mismatch-relevant field difference over the active region, not simply distance from a heater or absolute stress. Preserve useful symmetry under unequal power scenarios rather than assuming equal power forever. PDF pp. 399–411 , 525 , 715
reviews.supported_claim: Heat-source placement, thermoelectrics, piezoresistive stress and package environment constrain precision placement
reviews.detail: Read relevant thermal/stress implications; broad survey range is not a single geometric optimization theorem.

A smaller core may produce no die-area saving on a pad-limited chip; it may instead free area for lower resistance, extra taps, shielding or matching improvements. PDF pp. 782–810

reviews.original_attached_text: The book argues for optimizing the combined electrical consequences of interconnect, mismatch, and temperature. It explicitly criticizes converting the circuit specification into one fixed allocation of independent parasitic limits: a different allocation can produce an acceptable circuit that the original limits would reject. This is directly relevant to Philis’s per-net length budgets. A length limit is a useful implementable contract, but it is not, by itself, an electrical specification. PDF pp. 41–42

reviews.original_attached_text: The source writes the zero-reference special case. The sign matters: capacitance can worsen one metric and improve another, and coupling depends on the two connected nodes. A single positive “criticality” scalar cannot represent this entire matrix. The book reviews perturbation, direct sensitivity and adjoint sensitivity; it implements perturbation because of simulator availability. Finite differences trade truncation error against solver noise and require an appropriate perturbation size. Adjoint efficiency comes from many parameters sharing a scalar response; generally each independent scalar response needs its own adjoint solve, rather than accepting the book’s broad wording that two solves cover arbitrary numbers of responses. reviews.original_attached_text: Source finding. Position, orientation and shape constraints are different relationships. LAYLA uses separate move groups, allowing a position-symmetric pair to carry its own orientation rule and shape coupling. Symmetric translation, pair swapping, pair flipping, and moving the symmetry axis preserve relationships by construction. reviews.original_attached_text: Source finding. The source separates local defect faults from parametric variation. For a defect diameter χ bridging two long parallel conductors of overlap length L and spacing s, its simplified critical area is A(χ) = L·max(0, χ−s). Combining this with a defect-size density D(χ) gives expected fault count λ = ∫A(χ)D(χ)dχ; under the stated Poisson assumptions, the no-fault probability is exp(−λ). These formulas require calibrated defect mechanisms and geometrical approximations. They are not equivalent to mismatch yield. PDF pp. 153–157

reviews.original_attached_text: Dai, He, Xing, Chen, and Geiger construct a recursively symmetric layout for two identically designed devices. Starting with two units per device in a first-order pattern, the nth-order construction uses 2 n units per device and cancels polynomial parameter gradients through order n under the paper's additive unit model. The superscript matters: text extraction flattens it to “2n.” The claim concerns model cancellation; it does not establish best circuit performance or a universal minimum unit count. reviews.original_attached_text: The paper sums unit values for equal-size devices; the normalized moments above express the same result for equal counts and make ratio comparison easier to state. Second order also needs equal x², xy, and y² moments. Testing just radial distance checks x²+y² and can miss anisotropic x²−y² or xy fields. Equations (3)–(16), PDF pp. 2–3

reviews.original_attached_text: The measured bandgap output standard deviation is about 19 mV. The op-amp contribution dominates at about 18 mV output referred, corresponding to roughly 1.6 mV input offset; the parameter-based calculation gives roughly 1.7 mV input referred, with threshold-related mismatch dominant. Improving an already minor component cannot compensate for the dominant offset source. Conversely, large area increases become wasteful once another component sets the floor. The paper uses the model to estimate the area cost of a tighter reference specification; these numbers are an example of error budgeting, not a universal bandgap recipe. reviews.original_attached_text: A switching transistor can inject through source/drain junction capacitance and impact-ionization current. A well can isolate its devices when held at a quiet low-impedance potential, yet become a large capacitive injector if its potential bounces. Majority-carrier substrate taps and guard rings can similarly spread the noise of their reference connection. Passive devices also couple through their parasitic capacitance; diffusion resistors and capacitor bottom plates are not electrically invisible to the substrate. The reception mechanism determines the consequence: a MOS body voltage changes drain current through body transconductance, while a capacitive pickup drives the impedance of the receiving node. Chapter 2, PDF pp. 35–40 .
reviews.supported_claim: Substrate noise needs injection, propagation and reception, including other contacts and return paths.
reviews.detail: Checked Ch.1 global contact effects and Ch.2 junction/impact-ionization injection, well/tap bounce, capacitive reception and body effect. Conceptual n-well cross section is original; no PDK legality is implied.

reviews.original_attached_text: The complete contact network matters because injected current divides among all available return paths. Moving a tap can change voltages at distant receivers even if their separation from the original aggressor is unchanged. Include well contacts, rings, substrate ties, relevant junctions, backplate connections and their metal/package impedances. Contact depth, substrate doping profile, die boundaries and backside termination are inputs to extraction. Replacing this network with one independent resistor per aggressor-victim pair can miss the influence of third contacts. Global current paths, PDF p. 25 ; multi-port extraction, PDF pp. 44–49 .
