reviews.detail: Checked Ch.1 global contact effects and Ch.2 junction/impact-ionization injection, well/tap bounce, capacitive reception and body effect. Conceptual n-well cross section is original; no PDK legality is implied.

reviews.original_attached_text: This chapter follows Charbon, Gharpurey, Miliozzi, Meyer, and Sangiovanni-Vincentelli’s Substrate Noise: Analysis and Optimization for IC Design , especially chapters 2–5 and 7–8. Its extensive comparisons show why the substrate profile and the electrical return connection can reverse a seemingly reasonable layout choice. Physical paths ; Comparative isolation studies .
reviews.supported_claim: Spacing benefits depend on substrate/return structure; low-resistivity bulk with finite backside impedance can produce a separation plateau.
reviews.detail: §8.2.1 gives plateau and backside-inductance dependence; §8.2.2 contrasts high-resistivity surface current. Notes correctly avoid universalizing the example distances.

reviews.original_attached_text: The disturbance then propagates through substrate resistance, dielectric capacitance, well junctions, contacts, and the external return network. Package or bondwire inductance can let a large region of substrate move together. Finally, the victim converts local disturbance into error through body effect, junction capacitance, passive loss, common-mode conversion, or nonlinear mixing. The relevant voltage for a MOS body-effect path is often the body-to-source difference, not substrate voltage relative to an abstract ideal zero. Injection and reception, PDF 34–42 .
reviews.supported_claim: Substrate noise needs injection, propagation and reception, including other contacts and return paths.
reviews.detail: Checked Ch.1 global contact effects and Ch.2 junction/impact-ionization injection, well/tap bounce, capacitive reception and body effect. Conceptual n-well cross section is original; no PDK legality is implied.

reviews.original_attached_text: In a relatively high-resistivity substrate, lateral spreading resistance can make distance and surface guard contacts effective. In a low-resistivity substrate with an epitaxial layer, current can reach a conductive bulk region that couples distant locations. If that bulk region has a finite-impedance return, greater surface distance eventually offers limited improvement. The source shows this plateau behavior and its dependence on epitaxial thickness and backplate connection. Its example distances are not universal spacing rules. Substrate profile and separation, PDF 122–134 .
reviews.supported_claim: Spacing benefits depend on substrate/return structure; low-resistivity bulk with finite backside impedance can produce a separation plateau.
reviews.detail: §8.2.1 gives plateau and backside-inductance dependence; §8.2.2 contrasts high-resistivity surface current. Notes correctly avoid universalizing the example distances.

reviews.original_label: Buried shields and isolation structures, PDF 149–156
reviews.original_attached_text: A reverse-biased junction presents a capacitive barrier rather than perfect isolation. Deep wells, buried layers, and SOI structures change the paths and their frequency dependence. A smaller isolated region can reduce coupling capacitance but may crowd devices and routing. Well contacts must maintain the intended bias over DC, AC, startup, and disturbance conditions. Connecting a well to a nominal supply does not make it an AC ground if that supply has appreciable impedance or injected noise. Buried shields and isolation structures, PDF 149–156 .
reviews.supported_claim: Buried shields retain supply/ground-impedance and frequency-dependent limits.
reviews.detail: Old PDF149 anchor discussed differential guard rings. Corrected to §8.9 at PDF152–156.

reviews.original_label: Guard-ring return, width, and reference choice, PDF 139–147
reviews.original_attached_text: The same structure injects noise if its reference moves. At high frequency, a long wire or bondwire contributes jωL, so a contact network that looks excellent in DC can be ineffective or harmful in the operating band. A wider ring can lower local substrate resistance while leaving the inductive return unchanged; under some conditions this couples return noise more strongly into the victim. The source therefore finds cases where improving the connection is more valuable than widening the ring, and where a narrower ring with a better return is preferable. Guard-ring return, width, and reference choice, PDF 139–147 .
reviews.supported_claim: Guard-ring performance depends on ground reference, return inductance and geometry; a larger or noisily grounded ring can worsen error.
reviews.detail: Checked §§8.5–8.8, including internal/external observation reference and ring location. Original shared-return SVG is a conceptual KCL/impedance explanation, not a copied/source-tested layout.

reviews.original_attached_text: Two concentric rings with a shared noisy return are not equivalent to two independently quiet sinks. Separate returns can improve isolation in the source’s examples but consume pins and routing and eventually meet in the external network. The complete connection must be represented. Placing a ring around the aggressor can intercept injection before spreading; placing it around the victim can clamp the receiving region. Which is better depends on return noise, the substrate, aggressor/victim sizes, and pad locations. Location and multiple-ring tradeoffs .
reviews.supported_claim: Dual guard rings need genuinely separate returns to realize the source’s benefit.
reviews.detail: Old PDF143 citation was a single-ring width calculation. Changed to §8.8, PDF150–151. Ring-around-injector location discussion remains supported by §8.6.2 PDF144–147.

reviews.original_attached_text: Metal shields have the same dependence on reference quality. They can divert electric-field coupling into a reference path, but add capacitance and can import reference noise. A substrate shield or buried conductive layer with an ideal connection can look excellent in simulation and perform poorly once finite inductance is included. The correct comparison includes both direct metal coupling and substrate-mediated coupling, so improving one path is not mistaken for eliminating the total disturbance. Shield and connection impedance .
reviews.supported_claim: Buried shields retain supply/ground-impedance and frequency-dependent limits.
reviews.detail: Old PDF149 anchor discussed differential guard rings. Corrected to §8.9 at PDF152–156.

reviews.original_attached_text: For a linear isotropic electroquasistatic description, conduction and displacement currents satisfy a potential equation of the form ∇·(σ∇φ) + ∂/∂t[∇·(ε∇φ)] = 0. In sinusoidal analysis the material admittance is σ + jωε. A resistive approximation is appropriate only where displacement current is negligible over the relevant dimensions and spectrum. The relaxation time ε/σ helps assess this condition; there is no universal frequency cutoff for every substrate profile. Extraction equations and boundaries, PDF 44–54 .
reviews.supported_claim: Electroquasistatic substrate extraction uses conductivity/permittivity and explicit Dirichlet/Neumann/interface conditions.
reviews.detail: Eq.(3.1), resistive limit, Eq.(3.2), continuity Eq.(3.3), contact equipotential assumptions and boundary element formulation checked. No universal GHz cutoff or magnetic-field model is claimed.

reviews.original_attached_text: Finite-element methods handle complicated spatial material variation; boundary-element and Green-function methods can exploit layered homogeneous substrates efficiently. Mesh resolution and model reduction should be validated on the receiving transfer functions and circuit error, not only the norm of a large matrix. A reduced network must preserve relevant coupling, reference behavior, and passivity. The book’s fast-update and sensitivity methods are valuable for placement because moving one contact can modify a limited part of a coupling matrix. Their accuracy limits are empirical and depend on the move size and configuration. Incremental optimization, PDF 84–106 .
reviews.supported_claim: Incremental matrix updates and local sensitivity estimates can reduce search cost, with performance-weighted approximation control.
reviews.detail: Checked Sherman-Morrison discussion and local move-size errors, Eqs.(6.15)–(6.19), and cumulative conductance pruning. Notes do not turn empirical local accuracy into a global bound. Stronger-model verification policy is a handbook proposal.

reviews.original_attached_text: Switching noise depends on transition slew, load, supply impedance, simultaneous activity, and the relative time of transitions. The clock frequency alone does not describe the spectrum: fast edges excite much higher-frequency components. A useful source library stores cell or block injection waveforms under characterized load and supply conditions and combines them with activity scenarios. The book’s signature and convolution approaches reduce the cost of doing this repeatedly. Noise generation and simulation, PDF 56–68 .
reviews.supported_claim: Injection signatures depend on activity, slew, loading and supply conditions; iterative timing/noise refinement may fail to converge.
reviews.detail: Checked §§4.1–4.4 and two failure cases discussed on PDF65–66. Convolution/signature model is supported; unknown activity is not treated as a silent zero.

reviews.original_attached_text: The receiver may be linear around a bias point, periodically time varying, or nonlinear. A DC body sensitivity can be useful for low-frequency offset, but insufficient for an oscillator, sampler, mixer, or switched-capacitor circuit. The same substrate disturbance can create different jitter depending on its phase relative to an oscillator transition. Low-frequency substrate modulation can also mix with an RF carrier and create nearby spurs. Noise assessment therefore needs amplitude, spectrum, timing, and circuit state, not merely a peak substrate voltage. Sensitivity and phase-dependent jitter ; Circuit performance and RF effects .
reviews.supported_claim: Switching interference can affect jitter differently depending on phase relative to oscillator transitions.
reviews.detail: Changed generic PDF70 anchor to the actual §5.3 phase example. The static-mismatch-versus-temporal-noise distinction is instructional statistical interpretation, not presented as the book deriving all thermal/flicker noise laws.

reviews.original_attached_text: The receiver may be linear around a bias point, periodically time varying, or nonlinear. A DC body sensitivity can be useful for low-frequency offset, but insufficient for an oscillator, sampler, mixer, or switched-capacitor circuit. The same substrate disturbance can create different jitter depending on its phase relative to an oscillator transition. Low-frequency substrate modulation can also mix with an RF carrier and create nearby spurs. Noise assessment therefore needs amplitude, spectrum, timing, and circuit state, not merely a peak substrate voltage. Sensitivity and phase-dependent jitter ; Circuit performance and RF effects .
reviews.supported_claim: Substrate modulation can create in-band products by receiver nonlinearities and affect oscillator/sample behavior.
reviews.detail: Changed generic chapter introduction PDF108 to §7.4.3 PDF117–119.

reviews.original_attached_text: Two receivers that see equal transfer functions reject a shared disturbance in an ideal difference. Equality requires comparable substrate paths, body contacts, junction loading, well environment, wiring capacitance, and circuit sensitivities. Matching transistor centers while giving their body returns different impedances can defeat the benefit. A ring or well placed asymmetrically can also turn common-mode coupling into differential error. The source’s differential examples explicitly show imbalance limits. Differential structures and imbalance, PDF 131–134 .
reviews.supported_claim: Balanced differential coupling improves rejection, while receiver mismatch creates a residual floor.
reviews.detail: §8.3.2 explicitly models a 5% capacitor imbalance. vdiff=(H1−H2)va and −40dB/−80dB worked arithmetic are correctly identified instructional circuit derivations; complex transfer subtraction is required.

reviews.original_attached_text: A substrate transfer model linearized around reverse-biased junctions cannot certify behavior after a junction becomes forward biased, during an ESD event, or under a latchup trigger. Apply the PDK’s well enclosure, tap density/distance, injection-current, domain separation, voltage, and protection requirements independently. A configuration that gives excellent small-signal isolation can still violate a mandatory tap or well-bias rule. Conversely, passing latchup DRC does not establish the noise floor of a precision analog receiver. The source discusses protection-related injection as an additional path; detailed latchup and protection design requires the corresponding process/protection guidance. Circuit and protection coupling discussion .
reviews.supported_claim: Linear small-signal substrate models cannot certify nonlinear ESD behavior.
reviews.detail: Changed PDF108 to §7.4.4 PDF119–120. Latchup summary is a distinct protection-topic synthesis; it must not be cited as though this ESD passage proves the entire regenerative latchup mechanism.

reviews.original_attached_text: Validation should compare high- and low-resistivity substrate models, ideal and inductive backside returns, quiet and noisy ring references, single and double rings with shared versus separate returns, equal and unequal differential receiver loading, and an aggressor near a sensitive sampling instant. Verify mesh convergence, current conservation, reciprocity where the linear passive model implies it, and passivity of reduced networks. Compare against trusted extraction or measured test structures where available. The source’s measurement appendix warns that probe, pad, direct coupling, and measurement-floor limitations can obscure the substrate path, so fitting must include the measurement environment. Measurement techniques and limitations, PDF 170–182 .
reviews.supported_claim: Calibration requires suitable DC/RF structures and control of profile/contact/measurement-floor/package/direct-coupling errors.
reviews.detail: Appendix D supports error sources and the observed noisy guard-ring counterexample (PDF177–178,182). Reported source experiments are not claimed independently reproduced.

reviews.original_attached_text: This chapter combines the EM book’s coupled thermal/electrical/mechanical mechanisms with the mismatch papers’ sensitivity framework and the actual thermal model in Philis. The heat equations, numerical examples, and proposed algorithms below are instructional synthesis; they are not a claim that the supplied sources provide a complete foundry thermal deck. Thermal and stress migration ; Electrical sensitivity framework .
reviews.supported_claim: Diffusion depends on material interfaces; thermal and mechanical migration interact with electrical migration.
reviews.detail: Checked §§2.3.1,2.4.2,2.4.4,2.5 and 4.8. Separate back stress from external stress, and process-specific material behavior from universal constants. Relevant coupled fluxes are Eqs. (2.15)–(2.18), PDF54–55. Thermal chapter adds derived circuit implications.

reviews.original_attached_text: This chapter combines the EM book’s coupled thermal/electrical/mechanical mechanisms with the mismatch papers’ sensitivity framework and the actual thermal model in Philis. The heat equations, numerical examples, and proposed algorithms below are instructional synthesis; they are not a claim that the supplied sources provide a complete foundry thermal deck. Thermal and stress migration ; Electrical sensitivity framework .
reviews.supported_claim: First-order circuit sensitivity maps local perturbations to output error, and those sensitivities depend on bias.
reviews.detail: Drennan source supports the method. Applying it to deterministic rail drops or nonuniform thermal fields is an explicit handbook derivation/engineering synthesis; the paper does not supply the added thermal coefficients.

reviews.original_label: Coupled numerical and reduced modeling, PDF 58–69
reviews.original_attached_text: The source discusses analytical, lumped, and numerical thermal methods in the context of reliability. A hierarchy is useful: a cheap spreading model for placement search, a calibrated layered or reduced network for candidate evaluation, and a detailed field solve for critical or unusual structures. Accuracy should be judged against the temperature and electrical quantities that matter, rather than choosing the most expensive solver for every move. Coupled numerical and reduced modeling, PDF 58–69 .
reviews.supported_claim: Analytical, lumped and meshed approaches trade cost against spatial fidelity; coupled boundaries and template interfaces must be respected.
reviews.detail: Checked §2.6.1 and §§3.5.4–3.5.5. Numerical method descriptions are supported; thermal PDE/RC equations in handbook are energy-conservation/Fourier-law derivations, not equations asserted to appear in this EM passage. New precise Hastings citations support the thermal basis.

reviews.original_attached_text: Uniform temperature change does not always cancel even for a matched pair. Devices can have different biases, ratios, or surrounding circuitry; a resistor ratio can use materials with different temperature coefficients; an amplifier’s common-mode operating point can move. Compute the circuit sensitivity to both common and differential temperature modes. reviews.original_attached_text: Mirror routing can route one side against obstacles mirrored from both sides, but crossing differential nets need a balanced connector and matched layer transitions. Equal wirelength alone does not equalize coupling to asymmetrical neighboring nets. Shields need an appropriate low-impedance reference path; a floating or noisy shield can worsen the problem. Extraction accuracy should increase from simple estimates to detailed models as candidates mature; the chapter separately discusses RF interconnects, where inductance and transmission-line properties can be essential. reviews.original_attached_text: The routing survey distinguishes minimizing raw parasitics, enforcing allocated parasitic bounds, and optimizing sensitivity-derived performance costs. It also reviews interleaving routing with placement, constructing wires as movable layout objects, and templated routes. The LDS template example is particularly useful: independently preserving horizontal and vertical relations from one original layout can allow new overlaps after resizing; additional relations are needed to guarantee valid regenerated instances. Templates encode useful knowledge only if their valid parameter domain is checked. PDF pp. 182–193 , PDF pp. 198–203

reviews.original_attached_text: Source finding. Retargeting starts with an existing netlist/layout, target device dimensions, target technology and optional constraints. Layer mapping, recognition and constraint extraction precede compaction. A basic difference constraint x j −x i ≥ d ij fits a directed graph; longest paths in an acyclic ordering find the minimum legal coordinates. However, symmetry such as x b −x a = x d −x c involves four variables and does not fit an ordinary pairwise difference graph. The chapter’s coefficient-graph simplex retains general linear constraints while exploiting graph structure. PDF pp. 217–221 , PDF pp. 227–238
reviews.supported_claim: Pairwise difference compaction and general linear constraints have different expressive power; retargeting must preserve explicit intent and reverify target process.

reviews.original_attached_text: Important practical limitations include stale edge order after orthogonal compaction, long wires created by independently pushing edges, conditional wide-wire rules, well-proximity/STI effects, changed device aspect ratios, hierarchy and full device replacement. A source well larger than the minimum might embody deliberate electrical intent; shrinking it blindly can destroy that intent. Via-array aggregation can reduce constraints, but reconstruction must retain required current capacity and legal enclosure. PDF pp. 241–247

reviews.original_attached_text: Source finding. The chapter combines electrical sizing with a geometric-constraint module. For each candidate sizing, the module chooses geometric parameters such as finger counts and primitive shapes under a fixed template; the layout is generated or its parasitics estimated, then circuit performance is simulated. A bottom-up shape-function pass and top-down selection enforce aspect ratio and dimension goals. This recognizes that minimizing ΣWL does not necessarily minimize final layout area, especially after routing and spacing. PDF pp. 259–268
reviews.supported_claim: Fixed-template shape selection, actual or sampled parasitics and circuit simulation form a layout-aware sizing loop.

reviews.original_attached_text: Two parasitic approaches are compared: generate and extract actual template instances, or use analytical device geometry with precharacterized routing tables. A naïve table with m samples along n independent dimensions requires m n entries. The authors first identify important parasitics and then sample their influential parameters more densely. That is a useful strategy, but a table remains valid only for its technology, template, model conventions and characterized parameter domain. Its validity is not unconditional across future sizing runs. PDF pp. 272–275

reviews.original_attached_text: Source finding. The chapter separates technology, functional/electrical, methodological/geometric and commercial constraints. A required objective is a constraint; an optional “constraint” is an objective. It identifies five necessary services: management, derivation, transformation, sensitivity analysis and verification. DRC/LVS do not verify all analog intent, and a constraint that cannot be traced across hierarchy may be silently lost. PDF pp. 281–287

reviews.original_attached_text: A higher-level limit can admit several transformations. An IR-drop bound can be met by changing placement distance, layer, width or routing topology. Fixing one transformation too early discards alternatives; a generated bound therefore needs its parent relation and validity assumptions. Constraint sensitivity also depends on the current design: a width change may matter greatly for a narrow wire and little after widening. Derivatives of quantities with unlike units require normalization before ranking. PDF pp. 288–291

reviews.original_attached_text: The proposed constraint-engineering system uses logic rules, specialized solvers and adapters to external tools. Its lasting idea is decomposition: a high-level requirement selects relevant objects, obtains electrical/geometric facts, and evaluates the necessary relation. Philis does not need to adopt Prolog to preserve that architecture. Cheap structural failures can precede expensive simulation; static final verification must use a frozen design/constraint snapshot; dynamic optimization checks need cache invalidation after relevant changes.
